notes.title: Shaping canyons
notes.content:
Moving forward with developing Wasteland Arenas for Herogrinder, our next challenge was to make terrain level deformations, like trenches and gaps, using an approach that is compatible with our current Ground workflow. 

Here is how a trench will look on the map:

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35685129/decf49beb8bd99ee16e3e8abb3ce646849153372.png[/img]


For this, we made the trench geometry separately and treated it as a placeable asset.
Please note that this trench mesh is just a concept and only for testing purposes.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35685129/bfc6968cd33c14c169e436bd852af0c4821c1165.png[/img]


To be able to place it on the map, we have to tell our shader where the trench will be, so we mask out the terrain with a trench mesh shaped mask (the mask is rendered automatically).

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35685129/6434693b8c92b89568350945a0c7c6965090adfa.png[/img]


For the trench texture, at first we actually used the same shader as for terrain, leaving no visible seams between the ground mesh and the trench mesh.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35685129/6434693b8c92b89568350945a0c7c6965090adfa.png[/img]


The next step in this process is to properly design and model the trench meshes, completed with rocks, garbage, and radioactive waste.

notes.title: Herogrinder Map Editor Showcase
notes.content:
The most challenging part of designing the Wasteland Environment was how to make irregular and organic open environments on a constrained grid.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35685129/3dfd1d30c70e29454b8f9121db187bf861daf16a.png[/img]
After a few renders, it soon became clear that rocks, decals, and prop models are not enough, we have to improve the ground as well.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35685129/a7b9512f9e84aafab2a7094eeea2f07c44a0e3e2.gif[/img]
The Herogrinder Map Editor’s floor layer was originally designed for interiors: you can place small floor tiles onto to the grid.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35685129/b054537b500031ce8f13154d4bf6fb12116c90e8.png[/img]
One problem with the original workflow is the texture tiling size - interiors with repeating patterns look great, but for terrains, the current dense repeating pattern looks like a carpet, and not natural at all.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35685129/2f4d6b5ca5af010d08d8a0b7ffea383d6ac9a53e.gif[/img]
Another problem was the lack of blending between different textures. This wasn’t a problem for floor tiles in rooms but blending would be crucial outdoors for painting soil or dirt, mixing pebbles to road edges, and so on. 

Fixing the texture tiling issue was actually quite simple, due to the original workflow we developed for rendering the floor: 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35685129/15be7560178c3d941d8a43e520a0a7347a430cb0.png[/img]
The complete floor is one simple quad geometry, the tile textures stored in a Tex2DArray, and a point filtered controlmap tells the shader which pattern should be visible on the floor: one channel is used as a switch to tell if a cell is occupied with a floor texture, and another channel stores the index of that texture from the texture array. By using this texture mixing approach, the tiling of the floor tile textures is actually independent from the grid. Initially we simply just scaled the tiling of the tex2DArray to match the grid, but we have the freedom to set any tiling scale to them.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35685129/086230f89f93498ffa855c7814eed13d2d3bc5e5.gif[/img]
As we didn’t want to change the original floor workflow, we introduced a second ground layer: the Terrain. We set the tiling from 1x1 (this is what we use in the Floor layer) to a size of 4x4 grid tiles. For this terrain layer, we also designed a different set of textures.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35685129/cf99fc74c4b7f28201e133f4b4da2bcc2d63bcf0.gif[/img]
To blend terrain textures together, we have to use a different controlmap workflow: one channel used for each tile texture (0 - not visible at all and blending to 1 - completely visible), and we set the controlmap’s filtering to trilinear. 

This method enables us to use up to 5 terrain textures per level (an RGBA controlmap can hold up 4 textures, plus we can have one default texture, which is only visible if all channels are 0)  - which is more than enough for our Wasteland theme and per arena.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35685129/32f2fae47c4b519e102634bb8c1c1815d7008b6a.png[/img]
The last problem to resolve, is how to blend the floor layer and terrain layer together. This is still under development, and the most challenging part is achieving smooth, blended transitions, as well as sharp non-blending changes between the floor and terrain, together in one level. 

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35685129/d6c1f2bb915b5f4d843a816b9184aa3431256e8c.gif[/img]
One possible workaround to this problem is to keep hard edges between the floor and terrain, and to have a special set of decals: we call them terrain mask decals. Placing these decals in the right places, we can easily cover up the edge between floor and terrain. Terrain mask decals look exactly the same as the underlying terrain, but they cover the floor, and their mask acts as transparency, to make a nice looking transition between the terrain texture and the floor.

[img]{STEAM_CLAN_IMAGE}/35685129/47ca6278dada0a612f2729a1d83ca84922abbbe0.png[/img]
Having these great new features in our map editor makes it possible to design and develop Wasteland levels for Herogrinder with an organic feel and will allow us to use them on other themes as well.

notes.title: Wasteland arenas coming to life
notes.content:
After finishing up urban environments with the "Night Market" arena, that will feature both indoor and outdoor areas, and testing fully indoor Lab arena style, we have finally reverted to fully open-air environments that will be the hallmarks of the Wasteland arena style. 

These arenas are mostly located in former warzones that have been purchased by the New Horizons Media corporation to host Herogrinder battles. The main feature of these battle maps is their open natures, where walls will be scarce but longer range tactics can be utilized.

notes.title: Lab lighting styles
notes.content:
We are currently testing out lighting schemes for our arenas and after playing around with partially outdoor street environments with some indoor mall areas, we have moved onto fully indoor areanas like the labs.

Labs are unique for their sterile atmospheres, where crisp lighting is used. However, we wanted to see how different shaders and light textures would work. Also, emissive layers and depth effects add additional scopes to this project, so it is best to test all variations in a single layout.

[h1]OUR MAP EDITOR TOOL[/h1]

We did some shader experiments recently to find out how to achieve more variations to our environmental assets without changing or duplicating their diffuse textures. [h1]HEROGRINDER EVOLUTIONS: RAYCASTER[/h1]
To follow-up from our Herogrinder: Evolutions post a few months ago, we've decided to put the Raycaster into focus to showcase the full involvement of our entire team in the creation of a beautiful game asset. The Raycaster is a great example of the creative process behind Herogrinder, especially the game designers since it is a unique weapon that adds new game mechanics.

Instead of standard ammo and line of sight firing, the Raycaster emits an area effect that can target multiple enemies at the same time in either a line or a cone. The weapon is basically a point-and-fire solution that never misses and doesn't require an attack roll. As an energy weapon, it also negates recoil and can't fumble either. In addition, it also causes burn damage in succeeding rounds if the enemy can't avoid the flames.

Based on these specifications from game designers, our concept artist Luke drew the gun and we finalized the concept together. Then our 3D artist Gergo designed the object in 3D. Finally, our Unity team integrated it into the game environment and added it to the customizer.

We came full circle when the content team created the lore around the weapon and placed it into the context of the game, like so:

"[i]The Widerange Raycaster is the pride of Stellar Dynamics in the newest line from the “Spectrum series” developed in orbital factories under zero-g manufacturing protocols.
